cards.heading: Why this chapter exists
cards.body:
Picture this: it's registration week. A guy swears on his life he paid his fees. He's got the alert. But the portal says "not registered." The bank's copy says paid. The department's Excel sheet says something else entirely. Nobody's version agrees, and 400 students are now queuing outside one poor officer's desk who did NOT sign up for this today.

That's not "network wahala." That's what happens when nobody is managing information properly: records go missing, get duplicated, contradict each other, or just take forever to find. You've basically already lived Chapter 1 in real life — this is just the vocabulary for the disaster you already know.

cards.heading: The DIKW Pyramid
cards.body:
Think Spotify Wrapped. Spotify's servers logging "you streamed this song 1,847 times" is just raw Data — no context, no meaning.

When Wrapped tells you "you're in the top 0.5% of listeners for this artist," that's Information — same numbers, now with context.

When YOU notice "wait, I only run sad playlists during exam season" — that's Knowledge, you spotted a pattern.

When you go "let me build a hype playlist before finals so I don't spiral" — that's Wisdom, you used the pattern to make an actual decision.

**Data → Information → Knowledge → Wisdom** — each level adds meaning to the one below it.

Exam tip, stated directly on the slide: they want YOUR OWN example (banking, retail, health) — not Spotify, so don't try to recycle this one in the exam.

Official slide example, in case it shows up almost word-for-word: raw facts like 812, CSC201, 2025/2026, "MTR/25/0143" = Data. "812 students registered for CSC201" = Information. "CSC201 always fills up early" (a spotted pattern) = Knowledge. "Offer CSC201 twice next session" (an actual decision) = Wisdom.

cards.heading: What is Information Management?
cards.body:
It's the full job of handling information properly through its whole life: planning, capturing, organising, storing, protecting, retrieving and using it — right info, right people, right time, without wasting money doing it.

Here's the trap: it is NOT just "having a database." A database with zero rules around it is just an expensive place to lose things faster. IM is three things working together:
• **Policies** — who's allowed to see what, how long you're legally required to keep records
• **Processes** — how info gets captured, double-checked, corrected, eventually deleted
• **Technology** — the actual systems: files, DBMSs, search engines

A database with no policy is just chaos with better formatting.

cards.heading: The Information Lifecycle
cards.body:
Same shape as posting something online, honestly:

**Capture** (you take the photo) → **Organise** (caption it, tag people) → **Store** (post it / save it) → **Retrieve** (dig through your camera roll for it 8 months later) → **Use/Share** (repost, screenshot, send in the group chat) → **Archive/Dispose** (archive the story, or delete it because your ex is in it).

• Capture errors poison everything downstream — a blurry screenshot stays blurry forever (Ch.2)
• Retrieve speed depends on indexing — this is why searching your gallery by date works and scrolling doesn't (Ch.3)

Memorise this exact order — later chapters are literally built stage by stage around it.

cards.heading: Storage & Retrieval: three ideas that repeat all course
cards.body:
1. You never touch storage directly. A **DBMS** is the bouncer at the door — every request goes through it, which is exactly what keeps things secure and consistent instead of everyone editing raw files themselves.

2. The **index** is the shortcut. It's the difference between using Ctrl+F / a search bar and manually scrolling through 4,000 photos to find one. A small side-structure maps terms to locations so the system never has to scan everything (this comes back hard in Ch.3 and Ch.11).

3. Retrieval quality has two separate scores: **Effectiveness** (did you actually get the right answers?) and **Efficiency** (how fast, at what cost?). You can ace one and fail the other.

cards.heading: The six flavors of Information Management systems
cards.body:
Every system that touches information is built for one specific job. This is the actual diagram from the slide — six classes, know them cold:

• **TPS (Transaction Processing System)** — many fast writes, right now. e.g. course registration, fee payments — the debit alert energy from the next card.
• **MIS (Management Information System)** — routine, scheduled reports for management. e.g. "enrolment summary report," the boring weekly recap your class rep sends the HOD.
• **DSS (Decision Support System)** — answers one specific "what should we do?" question. e.g. "should we open a second CYB206 class since one filled up?"
• **BI (Business Intelligence System)** — dashboards of trends over time. e.g. performance dashboards, the VC watching enrolment trends across sessions.
• **IR (Search & Retrieval System)** — you search, it finds. e.g. the library catalogue, or literally Googling something.
• **RMS (Records Management System)** — long-term official records, rarely written, must always be trustworthy. e.g. transcripts, staff files, archives — your WAEC result 10 years later.

The classic mix-up on exams is MIS vs DSS: MIS = routine report on a schedule, nobody asked a specific question. DSS = someone asked a specific decision question and the system was built to answer THAT.

cards.heading: Transactional vs Analytical — the distinction that matters most
cards.body:
**Transactional (TPS)**: the debit alert that hits your phone the second you pay for suya. Many small, fast writes. Strict accuracy on every single record — nobody wants "maybe" as their bank balance. Current data only. Protected hard by **normalisation** (Ch.10). Example: the registration portal.

**Analytical (BI)**: your bank's "you spent 30% more this month" summary. Few, heavy reads over historical data, trends, KPIs. Often deliberately **denormalised** — the design rules get relaxed on purpose because speed over huge trends matters more than eliminating repeats (Ch.10). Example: the VC's enrolment dashboard.

Same underlying data, two completely different database designs depending on the job it's doing.

Another way to feel this one: BBNaija's 24/7 uncut live feed logging every single housemate action in real time is TPS energy — raw, constant, current. Sunday night's edited highlights-and-eviction show is BI energy — someone already crunched a week of footage into "here's what actually mattered." Same house, same housemates, two completely different jobs.

cards.heading: The running case study: Beacon University
cards.body:
One database, twelve chapters, zero mercy. You'll design it, build it in MySQL, query it, normalise it, tune it, deliberately break it, recover it, and defend it from SQL injection.

Domain facts (get formally modeled in Ch.6, so bank these now):
• A student belongs to one programme; a programme to one department
• Each semester a student registers for several courses; each course has many students
• A lecturer may teach several courses
• Every registration eventually gets a score and a grade
• Every fee payment must be traceable — no repeat of the opening scenario

quiz.question: A hospital dashboard shows "35% of ER patients this quarter were readmitted within 30 days." Which DIKW level is this?
quiz.explanation: It's Information: raw readmission records (Data) got context added by computing a meaningful percentage — like Spotify Wrapped turning stream counts into "top 0.5% listener." It'd only become Knowledge if it spotted a pattern (e.g. "readmissions spike among early-discharge patients"), and Wisdom if that pattern drove an actual decision (e.g. "extend observation time for high-risk patients").

quiz.question: Which of these is explicitly called NOT the full definition of Information Management?
options: Capture, store, retrieve throughout the info lifecycle
The right information to the right people, at the right time
quiz.explanation: The slides say it directly: IM is broader than "using a database." A database is just the technology piece — the bouncer with no rulebook. IM also covers policies (who can see what, retention rules) and processes (capture, verification, correction, disposal).

quiz.question: In the information lifecycle, which stage comes immediately before "Retrieve"?
quiz.explanation: The order is Capture → Organise → Store → Retrieve → Use/Share → Archive/Dispose. You have to store something durably before you can retrieve it.

quiz.question: What is the main job of an index in a retrieval system?
quiz.explanation: An index is a small side-structure mapping terms to locations, so a query can jump straight to the right rows instead of scrolling through your whole camera roll every time. Encryption, backups, and normalization are all separate concerns.

quiz.question: Beacon University's course registration portal — many small fast writes, strict integrity, current data — is an example of:
quiz.explanation: That description is the textbook definition of a Transactional (TPS) system — think debit alerts, not month-end summaries. BI/analytical systems are the opposite profile: few heavy reads over historical data, often denormalised on purpose.

quiz.question: True or False: Analytical (BI) systems are typically MORE strictly normalized than transactional systems, because accuracy matters more for decision-making.
quiz.explanation: False — it's the reverse. Transactional systems are strictly normalised to protect integrity on every single write. Analytical systems are often deliberately denormalised on purpose, because for BI, fast heavy reads over historical trends matter more than eliminating redundancy.

quiz.question: Your HOD's office runs a routine report every semester showing total enrolments per programme — nobody asked a specific question, it just runs on schedule. This is an example of a(n):
quiz.explanation: That's MIS — a routine, scheduled report for management oversight. It would be DSS instead if it existed to answer one specific decision question, like "should we open a second CYB206 class next session?" TPS handles live transactional writes (registration, payments); RMS is long-term archival records like transcripts.

quiz.question: Searching your school's online library catalogue for a textbook is an example of a(n):
quiz.explanation: That's an IR system — you search, it finds, same job as Googling something. RMS is about long-term official record-keeping (transcripts, staff files), not searching for something specific.

match.definition: Many fast writes, right now — e.g. course registration

cards.heading: One letter, two students
cards.body:
Registration week again, same Beacon University from Chapter 1 — except this time the mess isn't missing records, it's DUPLICATE ones. "Adaeze Ọkafor" exists TWICE in the admissions sheet:

• ADAEZE OKAFOR — typed by clerk 1
• Adaeze Okafor — typed by clerk 2
• Adaeze ?kafor — the Ọ died in a legacy encoding

And her JAMB number has a trailing space, so searches for it return nothing. No database was harmed in any of this — these are failures of CAPTURE and REPRESENTATION, and they happened before any database was ever reached. This chapter is about stopping them at the gate, before Chapter 1's whole resource-manager apparatus even gets involved.

cards.heading: The four capture channels
cards.body:
Information gets into a system through exactly four doors, each with its own failure mode:

• **Forms** — registration portals, paper forms. Risk: typos, inconsistent formatting (the Adaeze problem).
• **Transactions** — payments, till sales, bookings. Risk: duplicates, partial failures mid-transaction.
• **Devices** — sensors, scanners, biometrics. Risk: miscalibration, hardware noise.
• **Documents** — letters, reports, imports. Risk: unstructured mess that's hard to extract facts from.

All four funnel into the same next step — **Validation** — before anything touches Storage. Skip that step for ANY of the four doors, and garbage walks straight in.

cards.heading: GIGO — catch it at the gate, or don't catch it at all
cards.body:
**Garbage In, Garbage Out**: no later stage can fully repair bad capture. The cheapest place to catch an error is the exact moment it's typed — not during analysis, not during a report six months later. Four checks do almost all the work:

• **Type** — "score must be a number"
• **Range** — "score between 0 and 100"
• **Presence** — "matric number is required"
• **Uniqueness** — "no two students share a matric no" (the literal Adaeze bug)

Rule of thumb: capture SELECTIONS, not SPELLINGS — a dropdown physically cannot produce "B.Sc Data Sceince" as a typo, a free-text box can. Bank this idea: in Chapter 7 these exact four checks come back as actual database constraints — this is their first appearance, not their last.

cards.heading: The three shapes of data
cards.body:
Every piece of information has one of three shapes:

• **Structured** — fixed schema, rows and columns, every record has the same fields in the same order. e.g. database tables, spreadsheets, **CSV**.
• **Semi-structured** — flexible schema, tags and keys, records CAN differ (some have two phone numbers, some have none). e.g. **JSON**, **XML**.
• **Unstructured** — no predefined schema at all, meaning is buried inside free text, images, audio, or video. e.g. letters, emails, photos, lecture recordings.

Most organisations hold all three at once and have to manage all three. A WhatsApp voice note, a JSON payment receipt, the JAMB results table, and an NIN record are four different shapes sitting in the same phone.

cards.heading: Shapes convert in real workflows
cards.body:
Data doesn't stay one shape forever — it gets converted as it moves through a process. Classic example: an exam-appeal letter arrives as pure free text (**Unstructured**) → an officer reads it and extracts the key facts into a tagged summary (**Semi-structured**) → the final decision becomes one row in the appeals table (**Structured**).

This is genuinely most of what "data processing" even means: taking something messy and progressively shaping it until a database can hold it cleanly.

cards.heading: One record, three formats: CSV vs JSON vs XML
cards.body:
The exact same registration record, written three ways:

**CSV**: matric,course,session,score
MTR/25/0143,CSC201,2025/2026,74
+ compact, universal, opens in any spreadsheet — but flat only (no nesting), and commas inside data cause chaos.

**JSON**: { "matric": "MTR/25/0143", "course": "CSC201", "session": "2025/2026", "score": 74 }
+ handles nesting, lists, real data types, the language of web APIs — but wordier than CSV, no comments allowed.

**XML**: <registration><matric>MTR/25/0143</matric><course>CSC201</course><score>74</score></registration>
+ self-describing and validatable, strong in documents/standards — but the most verbose of the three.

All three are plain text, readable by humans AND by every programming language. None of them is "better" — they're optimized for different jobs.

cards.heading: Character encoding: why Ọkafor breaks
cards.body:
**ASCII** (1963) has exactly 128 characters. Fine for plain English. Completely useless for Ọkafor, Ádéwálé, or ₦ — those characters simply don't exist in ASCII's universe, so a system built on it either crashes, drops the character, or silently corrupts it into a "?".

**Unicode** + **UTF-8** fixes this properly: every character in every language, one universal encoding. The professional rule is non-negotiable: UTF-8 everywhere, end to end — files, database, application. In MySQL specifically, that means **utf8mb4**, not the older, narrower utf8. "Adaeze ?kafor" is exactly what you get when data gets written in one encoding and read back in another — the Ọ literally died in translation. This is why the resource-manager mindset from Chapter 1 matters even for something as "boring" as encoding — the OS/DBMS mediates this too.

cards.heading: Metadata: data about data
cards.body:
Metadata is the difference between a library and a pile of books. Three kinds:

• **Descriptive** — what it's about, for finding it. e.g. student name, session, keywords.
• **Structural** — how it's organised inside. e.g. "score is a number 0–100".
• **Administrative** — origin, history, permissions. e.g. captured by clerk #12, exams office access only.

Structural metadata specifically is a schema in embryo — in Chapter 4 it becomes the DBMS's actual data dictionary, managed automatically instead of just being a note someone wrote down.

cards.heading: From capture form to structured record
cards.body:
Watch what happens between what a user types and what actually gets stored. A student fills in: Full name, Matric no, Programme, Phone, Email. The system stores: student_id, full_name, matric_no, programme_id, phone, email.

Three quiet transformations happened:
• A hidden key got added (student_id) — this is a preview of **primary keys**, Chapter 7.
• A value became a code (programme becomes programme_id) — a preview of **foreign keys**, Chapters 7 & 10.
• Formats got normalised (the phone number) — for predictable matching later.

None of this was visible to the student filling the form. That invisibility is the whole point — capture should feel simple even when representation underneath is doing real work.

quiz.question: A biometric fingerprint scanner used at exam entry belongs to which capture channel?
quiz.explanation: Devices — sensors, scanners, biometrics. Forms are things users fill in, Transactions are payments/bookings, Documents are letters/reports being imported.

quiz.question: "The score must be a number" is an example of which type of validation rule?
quiz.explanation: Type validation — checking the kind of data, not its value. Range would be "between 0 and 100", Presence would be "this field can't be empty", Uniqueness would be "no duplicates allowed".

quiz.question: A WhatsApp voice note is an example of which shape of data?
quiz.explanation: Unstructured — no predefined schema, the meaning is buried inside audio with no fields or tags at all.

quiz.question: Which format is best described as "the language of web APIs" and handles nesting naturally?
quiz.explanation: JSON — compact, handles nested structures and lists naturally, and is what most web APIs speak. CSV is flat-only; XML is more verbose and document-oriented.

quiz.question: Why does "Adaeze Ọkafor" get corrupted into "Adaeze ?kafor" in some systems?
options: The server was down when it was typed
ASCII can't represent the character Ọ, but UTF-8 can
The student misspelled her own name
The course code was entered wrong
quiz.explanation: ASCII only has 128 characters and simply has no slot for Ọ. UTF-8 (specifically utf8mb4 in MySQL) covers every character in every language — the fix is encoding everywhere, end to end, not just in one layer.

quiz.question: In the capture-form-to-structured-record transformation, what typically gets ADDED that wasn't on the original form?
options: A hidden primary key like student_id
quiz.explanation: A hidden key (like student_id) gets added — the student never sees or types it, but it's what lets the record be uniquely and reliably referenced later. This previews primary keys properly in Chapter 7.

theory.question: Explain GIGO and describe the four types of validation rules used to catch bad data at the point of capture.
theory.modelAnswer: GIGO (Garbage In, Garbage Out) means that no later processing stage can fully repair data that was captured badly — the cheapest and most reliable place to catch an error is the exact moment it's typed. Four validation rules do most of the work: Type (is it the right kind of data, e.g. a number where a number is expected?), Range (does the value fall within acceptable limits, e.g. 0-100?), Presence (is a required field actually filled in?), and Uniqueness (is this value a duplicate where it shouldn't be, e.g. two students sharing a matric number?).
keyPoints: GIGO: bad data can't be reliably fixed later, catch it at capture
Type — correct kind of data
Range — value within acceptable limits
Presence — required field isn't empty
Uniqueness — no duplicates where they shouldn't exist

theory.question: Compare CSV, JSON and XML as ways to represent the same record, and explain when you'd choose each.
theory.modelAnswer: All three are plain-text formats representing the same data. CSV is compact and opens in any spreadsheet, ideal for flat tabular data, but can't handle nesting and breaks if the data itself contains commas — choose it for simple flat exports. JSON handles nesting, lists, and real data types naturally and is the standard language of web APIs — choose it when structure is more complex or when talking to a web service. XML is self-describing and strongly validatable, common in formal documents and industry standards, but the most verbose of the three — choose it when strict validation or document-style structure matters more than compactness.
keyPoints: CSV — compact, flat-only, spreadsheet-friendly, breaks on embedded commas
JSON — handles nesting/lists/types, standard for web APIs
XML — self-describing, strongly validatable, most verbose
Choice depends on the job: flat data vs API communication vs formal document standards

chapters.title: Analysis and Indexing: Search, Retrieval and Privacy — Topic 1

cards.heading: The search box that lied
cards.body:
Beacon University puts 8,000 past exam papers online with a search box. Students try it immediately.

Search "DATABASES" — zero results, even though dozens of papers have "Databases" right in the title. Every query takes a painful 11 seconds, because all 8,000 documents get scanned fresh every single time. And if a paper contains a student's personal appeal letter, anyone who guesses the right URL can read it — no login required.

Three completely different failures, three completely different fixes: no analysis, no indexing, no privacy controls. This chapter is all three.

Feels exactly like searching a WAEC result-checker portal for your own name in ALL CAPS and getting told "no record found."

cards.heading: Analysis: making text searchable
cards.body:
"DATABASES" found nothing because the search box did pure exact-string matching — no analysis step at all. Real search engines run every piece of text through a pipeline first:

Raw text → **Tokenise** (split into words: "Students PROTESTED the new Hostel fees!" becomes students | protested | the | new | hostel | fees) → **Normalise** (lowercase, drop stop-words like "the", stem protested → protest) → clean Index terms (student, protest, new, hostel, fee).

Skip this pipeline and a search for "DATABASES" will never match a title that says "Databases" — the computer sees them as two unrelated strings.

cards.heading: The inverted index — search's real engine
cards.body:
Once text is analysed into clean terms, they get flipped into an **inverted index**: instead of "document → words it contains", it's "word → which documents contain it" (a **postings list**).

Three mini-documents — D1: "hostel fees increased", D2: "students protest fees", D3: "new hostel opened" — produce an index like fee → D1,D2 and hostel → D1,D3.

Query "hostel fees"? Look up both terms, intersect their postings lists, get D1. No document was scanned. This is exactly the step Beacon's search box skipped, which is why it was slow AND wrong.

cards.heading: The B+-tree — the database's shortcut
cards.body:
Text search uses inverted indexes; structured lookups (like finding one student by matric number) use a different structure: the **B+-tree**.

Without one, finding MTR/25/0145 means a **full table scan** — checking row 1, row 2, row 3... every row, in order, until it's found. With a B+-tree index, the database follows a few signposts instead: is it ≤M or >M? A-F/G-M or N-S/T-Z? A handful of branches later, it's sitting right at the row.

The payoff is dramatic: 1,000,000 rows ≈ 20 checks with an index, not 1,000,000. The index itself is smaller than the data and lives beside it — a bit of storage traded for a lot of speed.

cards.heading: EXPLAIN doesn't lie: watching a query before and after an index
cards.body:
Talk is cheap. MySQL's **EXPLAIN** command is the receipt that proves whether an index actually did anything, and it's the single most exam-tested habit in this whole chapter.

Before indexing, run EXPLAIN on a search across Beacon's 100,000+ row student table and the type column reads ALL — MySQL's polite way of admitting "I checked every single row, one by one," with a rows estimate matching the table's full size. That's the full-scan disaster from earlier in this chapter, now with a timestamp attached.

Run CREATE INDEX on the searched column, then EXPLAIN the exact same query again: type changes to something far cheaper (ref or range, not ALL), the rows estimate collapses from six figures to a tiny handful, and the actual timing drops to match. Divide the old time by the new time and you have a real, defensible speed-up factor — not a guess, a measurement.

cards.heading: LIKE vs. MATCH…AGAINST: two very different kinds of 'search'
cards.body:
`LIKE '%hostel%'` against a free-text column forces MySQL back into a full scan every single time — there's no index that can help a wildcard sitting on BOTH sides of the search term, so it's reading every row's text character by character, checking for a match, no shortcuts available.

`MATCH(body) AGAINST('hostel')` against a **FULLTEXT** index is a completely different animal — it's the **inverted index** from earlier in this chapter, actually being used, and it doesn't just return a yes/no, it returns a relevance score ranking how well each document matches, best answers first. This is exact-match's evil twin from the "two ways to answer a query" card, made concrete: LIKE forces exact-string full-scanning, MATCH…AGAINST gives you real ranked retrieval, and the two can return meaningfully different result sets for the exact same search term on the exact same data.

cards.heading: Two ways to answer a query
cards.body:
Not every search works the same way:

• **Exact-match (Boolean)** — returns everything that satisfies a condition, no more, no less, unranked. Natural for structured data: WHERE matric_no = '...' either matches or it doesn't.

• **Ranked retrieval** — scores every document by relevance and returns the best answers first. Natural for text: a search engine, or MATCH...AGAINST in SQL.

Beacon's exam-paper search needed ranked retrieval ("which papers best match this topic?") but was built like exact-match — another reason it felt broken.

cards.heading: Measuring effectiveness: precision and recall
cards.body:
"Good search results" isn't a feeling — it's measured. Picture two overlapping circles: everything Retrieved (what the system returned) and everything Relevant (what the user actually wanted). Where they overlap: True hits.

• **Precision** = hits ÷ retrieved — "how clean are my results?" (no noise)
• **Recall** = hits ÷ relevant — "how much did I find?" (miss nothing)

They pull against each other. A plagiarism checker chases recall — missing one copied paragraph is a disaster, a little noise is fine. A top-3 answer box chases precision — three wrong answers ruins it, so nothing loose gets shown.

Same tension as searching a trending topic on X (Twitter): too much noise mixed in with the real gist is a precision problem, missing the actual gist entirely is a recall problem.

cards.heading: Privacy is law: the NDPA 2023
cards.body:
Beacon's leaky exam-appeal URLs weren't just embarrassing — they were illegal. The **Nigeria Data Protection Act (2023)** binds every organisation processing personal data, universities included, and mirrors the EU's GDPR. Seven principles:

• **Lawfulness & transparency** — tell people what you do with their data
• **Purpose limitation** — use it only for what it was collected for
• **Data minimisation** — collect only what you need
• Accuracy — keep it correct; let people fix it
• **Storage limitation** — don't keep it forever without reason
• **Integrity & confidentiality** — secure it, no guessable URLs
• **Accountability** — be able to prove all of the above

cards.heading: Privacy for designers: two habits and one trap
cards.body:
Turning the NDPA's principles into actual design habits:

• **Minimise** — every column you don't collect is a column you can't leak
• **Control access** — decide who may see what (the security machinery of Chapter 12)

And the trap: removing names is NOT **anonymisation**. Beacon could strip every student's name from a leaked table and it would still be identifiable — matric number + birth date + programme, combined, can point to exactly one person even with the name gone. Real anonymisation has to think about combinations of fields, not just the obviously personal ones.

This is exactly why Nigerians got nervous when BVN details started turning up linked across different apps — a name alone doesn't feel dangerous, but name plus account number plus date of birth suddenly identifies one specific person, no guessing required.

cards.heading: Efficiency, effectiveness, scalability — three dials in tension
cards.body:
Three separate questions, easy to confuse:

• Efficiency — the cost of one operation (time, memory, money). Indexing means the same answer for fewer resources.
• Effectiveness — are the answers actually right? Measured by precision and recall. Scanning everything is effective, but it's inefficient.
• **Scalability** — what happens to efficiency as volume grows. Fast at 5,000 students but unusable at 50,000 students is NOT scalable.

Growth has two paths: **scale up** (a bigger machine — has a ceiling) or **scale out** (more machines — coordination gets hard, covered in Chapters 8 and 12). Beacon's search box failed all three dials at once.

quiz.question: Beacon's search box returned zero results for "DATABASES" even though papers titled "Databases" existed. What pipeline step was missing?
quiz.explanation: Analysis — without tokenising and normalising (e.g. lowercasing), the system treats "DATABASES" and "Databases" as two completely unrelated strings instead of the same search term.

quiz.question: What does an inverted index actually store?
options: Each document mapped to the words it contains
Each word mapped to the list of documents that contain it
A backup copy of every document
A ranked list of the most popular searches
quiz.explanation: An inverted index flips the natural direction: word → postings list of documents. A query becomes a fast lookup-and-intersect instead of scanning every document.

quiz.question: Roughly how many checks does a B+-tree index need to find one row among 1,000,000, compared to a full table scan?
options: The same as a full scan
quiz.explanation: About 20 — following the tree's signposts (branch by branch) needs only a handful of hops, versus checking all 1,000,000 rows one by one in a full table scan.

quiz.question: A query like `WHERE matric_no = 'MTR/25/0145'` is a natural fit for which retrieval style?
quiz.explanation: Exact-match — the condition is either satisfied or it isn't, no ranking involved. Ranked retrieval is for text search, where results are scored by relevance.

quiz.question: A plagiarism checker cares most about not missing a single copied passage, even if it flags some innocent ones too. Which measure is it optimising for?
quiz.explanation: Recall (hits ÷ relevant) — "how much did I find?" A little noise (lower precision) is an acceptable trade-off for not missing real matches.

quiz.question: Beacon strips student names from a leaked table but leaves matric number, birth date, and programme intact. Is this data properly anonymised under the NDPA?
options: Yes, removing names is the standard for anonymisation
No, that combination of fields can still identify someone
Yes, as long as the URL isn't shared publicly
No, but only because the NDPA requires encryption too
quiz.explanation: No — this is the anonymisation trap. Matric number, birth date, and programme combined can still point to exactly one person even with the name gone; real anonymisation has to consider combinations of fields, not just names.

quiz.question: Before creating an index, EXPLAIN on a search query shows `type: ALL` with a rows estimate matching the whole table. What does this tell you?
options: The query is already using an index efficiently
MySQL is doing a full table scan, checking every row one by one
The query contains a syntax error
quiz.explanation: `type: ALL` is MySQL's way of reporting a full table scan — every row gets checked, which is exactly the full-scan disaster indexing exists to fix.

quiz.question: Why can't `LIKE '%hostel%'` use a normal index, even if one exists on that column?
options: LIKE queries are not valid SQL
A wildcard on both sides of the search term means MySQL can't jump to a starting point in the index — it still has to check every row
Indexes only work on numeric columns
LIKE always returns zero results on text columns
quiz.explanation: A leading wildcard (`%hostel%`) means there's no fixed prefix to look up in an index's sorted order, forcing MySQL back into a full scan — this is exactly why FULLTEXT + MATCH...AGAINST exists as the real alternative.

theory.question: Using Beacon's "Search Box That Lied" scenario, identify the three separate failures it demonstrates (analysis, indexing, privacy) and explain what each one should have done differently.
theory.modelAnswer: The scenario shows three unrelated failures happening at once. First, an analysis failure: searching "DATABASES" found nothing because the system did pure exact-string matching instead of tokenising and normalising text, so it never recognised "DATABASES" and "Databases" as the same term. Second, an indexing failure: every query took 11 seconds because all 8,000 documents were scanned from scratch each time, instead of using an inverted index to look up matching documents directly. Third, a privacy failure: any exam result slip was readable just by guessing its URL, because there was no access control on personal data — a direct violation of the NDPA's integrity & confidentiality principle. Each failure needed its own fix; none of them would have solved the other two.
keyPoints: Analysis failure — no tokenise/normalise, exact-string matching only
Indexing failure — full scan every query, no inverted index
Privacy failure — no access control, guessable URLs

theory.question: State the NDPA 2023's core privacy principles and explain the 'anonymisation trap' that designers need to watch for.
theory.modelAnswer: The Nigeria Data Protection Act (2023) sets seven principles for any organisation processing personal data: lawfulness & transparency (tell people what you do with their data), purpose limitation (use data only for what it was collected for), data minimisation (collect only what's needed), accuracy (keep it correct, allow corrections), storage limitation (don't keep it forever without reason), integrity & confidentiality (secure it, no guessable URLs), and accountability (be able to prove all of the above). The anonymisation trap is the mistaken belief that removing names alone makes data anonymous — in reality, a combination of other fields (like matric number, birth date, and programme) can still uniquely identify a person even without their name attached, so real anonymisation has to consider how fields combine, not just which ones are obviously personal.
keyPoints: Lawfulness & transparency
Purpose limitation
Data minimisation
Accuracy
Storage limitation
Integrity & confidentiality
Accountability
Anonymisation trap — names-off isn't enough, combinations can still identify someone

cards.heading: The night two clerks pressed Save
cards.body:
Same Beacon University, registration week. Registry and Bursary are both editing the same shared file, students.xlsx.

9:41 pm — Registry saves: +43 late registrations.
9:44 pm — Bursary saves too, from an older copy she'd downloaded earlier that day.

Her Save wins. Registry's 43 students are gone — not deleted on purpose, just quietly overwritten. Nobody notices for three weeks. There's no log of who did what, no fresh backup, and now three different files each claim to be "the real student list."

This is what happens when "the database" is just a spreadsheet everybody keeps a personal copy of.

cards.heading: One gatekeeper vs. everybody for themselves
cards.body:
File-based approach: Registry writes students.xlsx, Bursary writes payments.xlsx AND her own students2.xlsx, Exams writes results.csv AND student_list.csv. Same student, three copies — which one is true? Nobody's app talks to any other app.

Database approach: Registry, Bursary and Exams all go through ONE piece of software — the DBMS — which owns ONE database. The DBMS is the single gatekeeper for every read and write.

"**One copy of the truth, shared by all**." That's the entire pitch of a database system, and it's what would have stopped the 9:44 pm disaster before it started.

cards.heading: Six ways a spreadsheet betrays you
cards.body:
The classic file-system failures, each one visible in the Beacon scenario:

• **Redundancy** — same fact stored in many places (students.xlsx AND student_list.csv)
• **Inconsistency** — the copies disagree (Registry, Bursary and Exams all differ)
• **Lost updates** — edits silently overwrite each other (the 9:44 pm save)
• **No atomicity** — a change half-happens (a programme transfer updates one file, then crashes)
• **Data isolation** — a combined question needs manual file-hunting ("unpaid fees by programme" means opening 3 files by hand)
• **Weak integrity, security & recovery** — a score of 250 gets accepted, and nobody catches it for 3 weeks

Exam favourite: each of these six failures pairs with exactly one DBMS function — that's next.

cards.heading: It's not just software
cards.body:
A database system has five components, not one:

• **Hardware** — the machine it runs on
• **Software** — the DBMS itself
• Data — the actual facts being stored
• **Procedures** — the documented rules people are supposed to follow
• **People** — everyone who touches the system

Beacon's disaster wasn't a broken laptop or buggy software. It was a missing procedure — no rule for who saves last, no backup routine — carried out by people who had no way of knowing they'd just erased each other's work. Procedures fail as often as technology.

cards.heading: What that gatekeeper actually does
cards.body:
A DBMS is "software that manages all access" to the database. Its core functions:

• **Data storage** — organises the files and pages on disk
• **Data dictionary** — tracks metadata: tables, columns, types, rules, permissions
• **Query processing** — parses and optimises SQL
• **Integrity** — enforces the rules (no 250 out of 100, no duplicate matric numbers)
• **Security** — controls who's even allowed to log in and see what
• **Concurrency** — lets many users work at once without chaos
• **Backup & recovery** — survives crashes instead of just losing data
• **Transactions** — all-or-nothing changes, no half-done updates

Every one of these replaces code that file-based apps would otherwise have had to write badly, themselves, from scratch.

cards.heading: Beacon's disaster, function by function
cards.body:
Match every failure from the scenario to the exact DBMS function built to stop it:

• **Lost updates** → **Concurrency** control
• Half-done changes → **Transactions** (all-or-nothing)
• Score of 250 / duplicate matric number → **Integrity** enforcement
• Anyone reads everything → **Security** management
• Three weeks, unrecoverable → **Backup & recovery**
• "Which file is true?" → One database + a data dictionary

Nothing about the DBMS is decorative — every single function on the list exists because some real spreadsheet, somewhere, failed exactly that way first.

cards.heading: From using the database to owning it
cards.body:
Database people split into classes, from lightest touch to heaviest responsibility:

• **End users** — use apps, never see SQL (e.g. a student on the registration portal)
• **Analysts** — query and report with SQL / BI tools (e.g. enrolment dashboards)
• **Developers** — build the applications (e.g. write the portal's code)
• **Designers** — model the schemas: tables and keys (Chapter 6)
• **DBA** — owns the running system: security, backups, tuning

In a small Nigerian firm, one person often wears several of these hats at once — the "developer" and the "DBA" might be the same overworked person.

This is exactly how small Nigerian fintech teams run in real life — the same person building the Paystack integration today might be the one restoring the database backup at 2 a.m. next week.

cards.heading: Best for what, not best
cards.body:
The DBMS landscape you'll actually meet:

• **MySQL** — relational, open source, everywhere on the web (this course's labs)
• **PostgreSQL** — relational, open source, rigorous and extensible (startups, analytics)
• **Oracle** — relational, commercial, enterprise muscle (banks, telcos, government)
• **SQL Server** — relational, commercial, Microsoft ecosystem (corporate Windows shops)
• **SQLite** — relational, zero-server, a single file (phones, embedded apps)
• **MongoDB** — document-based (NoSQL), flexible JSON-style schema (APIs, changing data)

The exam trap is asking "which is best?" There's no such answer — only "best for what?"

Same energy as the Opay-vs-PalmPay-vs-Moniepoint arguments on Naija Twitter — everyone insists theirs is "the best," but the honest answer is always "best for what you're actually doing with it."

cards.heading: An untested backup is a hope, not a backup
cards.body:
If Bursary's 9:44 pm overwrite had hit a real DBMS instead of a shared spreadsheet, backup & recovery would have made the 43 students recoverable in minutes.

But a backup file sitting untouched on a drive isn't proof of anything. You don't actually know it works until you've restored it somewhere else and checked the data comes back intact — which is exactly what Lab 3A has you do: dump beacon_uni, restore it into a copy database, and prove it. "**An untested backup is a hope, not a backup**."

Like keeping a generator you've never actually test-started — you only find out it's faulty the moment NEPA takes light and you actually needed it to work.

quiz.question: In the Beacon University scenario, Bursary's 9:44 pm save silently erased Registry's 43 new registrations. Which classic file-system failure is this?
quiz.explanation: Lost update — two people editing overlapping data, and the last write silently discards the other's changes. Redundancy is having many copies of the same fact; inconsistency is when those copies disagree; data isolation is when a combined question needs manual cross-referencing across files.

quiz.question: Which of the five components of a database system is most easily overlooked, yet "fails as often as technology"?
quiz.explanation: Procedures — the documented rules for who saves last, when backups run, how conflicts get resolved. Beacon's disaster wasn't a broken laptop or bad software; it was a missing procedure.

quiz.question: Which DBMS function guarantees that a programme-transfer update either fully completes or doesn't happen at all, never leaving a student half-transferred?
quiz.explanation: Transactions — all-or-nothing changes. This is exactly what prevents "no atomicity" failures, like a crash mid-update leaving data in a broken in-between state.

quiz.question: Which class of database user interacts only through an app's interface and never writes SQL directly?
quiz.explanation: End users — they use the registration portal and never see a query. Analysts query and report, developers build the applications, and the DBA owns the running system.

quiz.question: Which DBMS in the landscape is known for a flexible, JSON-style document model rather than the traditional row-and-column table?
quiz.explanation: MongoDB — a document (NoSQL) database built around flexible JSON-style records, common for APIs and data whose shape keeps changing.

quiz.question: What's wrong with a backup that was taken but never restored anywhere to check it actually works?
options: Nothing — a backup is a backup
It isn't a real backup yet, it's just a hope
It only matters for hardware failures
quiz.explanation: "An untested backup is a hope, not a backup." You don't actually know it works until you've restored it somewhere else and proven the data comes back intact.

theory.question: Using the Beacon University 9:44 pm scenario, name at least three of the classic file-system failures it demonstrates, and explain how a DBMS's functions would have prevented each one.
theory.modelAnswer: The scenario shows several failures at once. The 9:44 pm overwrite is a lost update — Bursary's save silently discarded Registry's 43 new registrations; a DBMS's concurrency control would have detected the conflict instead of letting one save blindly clobber the other. The three disagreeing files (students.xlsx, student_list.csv, and Bursary's own copy) are redundancy and inconsistency — a DBMS replaces all of them with one shared database, so there's only ever one copy to disagree with itself. And the fact that nobody noticed for three weeks with no way to recover the lost data is a backup & recovery failure — a DBMS with proper, tested backups could have restored the 43 students in minutes instead of losing them for good.
keyPoints: Lost update — concurrency control
Redundancy/Inconsistency — one shared database
No atomicity — transactions
Weak recovery — backup & recovery

theory.question: Describe the five components of a database system, and explain — using the Beacon scenario — why 'procedures' and 'people' matter just as much as hardware and software.
theory.modelAnswer: The five components are hardware (the machine it runs on), software (the DBMS itself), data (the actual facts stored), procedures (the documented rules people are supposed to follow), and people (everyone who touches the system). Beacon's disaster is a clean example of why the last two matter: the hardware worked fine and the spreadsheet software worked exactly as designed — the failure was that there was no procedure telling Bursary to check for a newer version before saving, and no person had been made responsible for coordinating who saves when. A database system with perfect hardware and software still fails if its procedures and people aren't accounted for.
keyPoints: Hardware
Software (the DBMS)
Data
Procedures
People

cards.heading: The upgrade nobody noticed
cards.body:
One weekend, Beacon's ICT team quietly moved the entire database to a new server, changed how three of the biggest tables are physically stored, and added a fresh set of indexes. Monday morning: 4,000 students logged in, Bursary pulled their reports, Exams ran their summaries — and not one line of application code had to change.

That's not luck. Compare it to what would have happened in Chapter 4's file-based world, where moving students.xlsx to a new folder used to break every single macro pointing at it. This chapter is about the actual engineering trick that makes "we changed everything underneath and nobody felt it" a completely normal Monday instead of a minor miracle: a 1970s architectural idea that's still quietly running the show.

cards.heading: The three-schema architecture: you've already touched all three
cards.body:
The ANSI/SPARC three-schema architecture splits a database into three honest layers, and you've been living in all of them without necessarily naming them:

**External** — "what does THIS user group see?" Bursary's view shows students + payments, no grades. Exams' view shows students + results, no payment data. A student logging into the portal sees only their own records. Many views, each cropped to what that audience actually needs.

**Conceptual** — "what exists, and how does it relate?" One single logical schema underneath all those views: every table, every column, every rule, the whole design a database designer draws in Chapter 6 and 7.

**Internal** — "how is it physically stored?" The messy, unglamorous reality: .ibd files, B+-tree indexes, InnoDB pages, buffer pools — the DBMS and the DBA's actual job.

Three separate questions, three separate layers, and the entire trick of this chapter is that changing one almost never disturbs the other two.

cards.heading: Data independence: the actual payoff
cards.body:
This is the entire point of splitting into three layers, not just a tidy diagram for its own sake. **Physical independence** means the DBA can change HOW data is stored — new server, new file layout, a fresh index — and every application built on top keeps working, completely unaware anything moved. That's exactly what happened in the weekend upgrade.

**Logical independence** means the conceptual schema can grow — a new column, a new table — without breaking the views and applications sitting on top of it, as long as the change is additive rather than destructive.

Without this separation, every storage tweak would ripple straight up into broken code, the way renaming a folder used to break Beacon's old spreadsheet macros. With it, an entire category of Monday-morning disasters simply stops being possible.

cards.heading: The designer's moral: extend, don't rewrite
cards.body:
Not every change is equally safe, and the three-schema architecture won't save you from a reckless one. **Additive change** is cheap: ADD COLUMN email and every existing view survives untouched; a brand new table means nothing else even notices; a new index gives the same answers, just faster.

**Destructive change** ripples straight through the layers: DROP a column a view still depends on, and that view breaks. Rename a table an application points at, and that application breaks. Split a table other queries JOIN to, and every one of those queries breaks.

The professional habit this teaches: design conservatively. Extend the schema outward rather than rewriting what's already load-bearing — the three-schema architecture only protects you from the storage layer changing underneath you, not from you personally taking a wrecking ball to the conceptual layer everyone else depends on.

cards.heading: Where the software actually runs: 1, 2, 3 tiers
cards.body:
**1-tier (desktop)** — the app, the DBMS, and the data all live on one single machine, talking to nobody. SQLite on a phone, Access on one PC. No architecture drama, because there's nobody else to protect from your changes.

**2-tier (client-server)** — a client app (Workbench, a POS terminal) talks directly to a separate database server over the network. This is exactly the lab setup used throughout this course, and how a lot of real office systems run.

**3-tier (web)** — a browser or mobile app talks to an application server (the actual portal), which is the only thing that talks to the database server. Users never touch the database directly in this model — the middle tier holds the business rules AND the credentials, which is exactly how the Beacon portal itself, and most web apps you've ever used, are actually built.

cards.heading: Cloud databases: renting the internal level
cards.body:
A cloud database provider owns the hardware, the disks, the backups, the replication, the patching — everything sitting below the physical-independence firewall this chapter just spent three cards explaining. In three-schema terms: they've taken over the ENTIRE internal level and rented it back to you.

What you still own, and what this whole course has actually been teaching: the conceptual design, the views, the SQL, the integrity rules. The provider changing which physical disk your data sits on, or migrating you to new hardware overnight, is precisely the kind of invisible internal-level change the three-schema architecture was built to absorb — which is the entire reason "renting a cloud database" is even a coherent business model in the first place, and not just a recipe for constant breakage.

This is exactly the pitch behind every Nigerian startup now building on AWS or Google Cloud instead of buying their own server rack — the founders never touch a physical disk, and the three-schema architecture is precisely why that's a safe bet, not a leap of faith.

cards.heading: Four language families, one SQL
cards.body:
Every SQL statement you'll ever type belongs to exactly one of four families, and knowing which tells you both what it does and who's normally allowed to run it:

**DDL (Data Definition Language)** — defines structure: CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE, CREATE INDEX. Touches the conceptual and internal levels, usually a designer or DBA's job.

**DML (Data Manipulation Language)** — works with the actual data: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE. The everyday tool for anyone querying or updating rows.

**DCL (Data Control Language)** — controls access: GRANT, REVOKE. Squarely a DBA's territory — deciding who's allowed to do any of the above.

**TCL (Transaction Control Language)** — manages transactions: COMMIT, ROLLBACK. The seatbelt language, covered properly in Chapter 12.

`REVOKE INSERT ON payments FROM 'clerk';` is DCL. `ALTER TABLE students DROP COLUMN email;` is DDL. `ROLLBACK;` is TCL. `UPDATE results SET score = 74 WHERE reg_id = 55;` is DML. Four families, one language, and naming the family on sight is exactly the kind of question this chapter loves to ask.

quiz.question: Beacon's ICT team moved the database to a new server and added new indexes over a weekend, and zero application code broke on Monday. Which concept explains this?
options: The internal schema alone, with no other layers involved
quiz.explanation: Physical data independence — the ability to change HOW data is physically stored without affecting the applications built on top, exactly what let the weekend upgrade go unnoticed.

quiz.question: Bursary's view shows students + payments with no grades visible, while Exams' view shows students + results with no payment data. Which schema level do these views belong to?
quiz.explanation: External — the level that answers 'what does this specific user group see?' Multiple different views, each cropped to what that audience needs, all built on top of the same single conceptual schema.

quiz.question: Which of these is an example of a DESTRUCTIVE change that would ripple through the three-schema architecture, rather than an additive one?
options: Adding a new email column to the students table
Creating a new index on an existing column
Dropping a column that an existing view depends on
quiz.explanation: Dropping a column a view depends on is destructive — it breaks anything built on top of that column. Adding columns, tables, or indexes are all additive changes that existing views and applications survive untouched.

quiz.question: In a 3-tier web architecture, why does the user's browser never talk to the database server directly?
options: Browsers are technically incapable of running SQL
The application server (the middle tier) holds the business rules and the credentials, and is the only thing that talks to the database
3-tier architecture doesn't actually use a database at all
It would make the database run faster
quiz.explanation: The application server sits in the middle specifically to hold business logic and database credentials, so users never get direct database access — exactly how the Beacon portal itself, and most web apps, are actually built.

quiz.question: A cloud database provider handles hardware, disks, backups, and patching. Which schema level have they effectively taken over?
options: None — cloud providers don't map onto the three-schema architecture
quiz.explanation: The internal level — everything about physical storage and hardware. You still own the conceptual design, views, SQL, and integrity rules, which is exactly the skill set this course teaches.

quiz.question: `GRANT SELECT ON students TO 'analyst';` belongs to which SQL language family?
quiz.explanation: DCL (Data Control Language) — statements that control access, like GRANT and REVOKE, squarely a DBA's territory for deciding who's allowed to do what.

theory.question: Explain the three-schema architecture (external, conceptual, internal), and use Beacon's weekend server upgrade to illustrate exactly which layer changed and why nothing above it broke.
theory.modelAnswer: The three-schema architecture splits a database into three layers answering three separate questions. The external level answers 'what does this specific user group see?' — Beacon has multiple views here, like Bursary's students+payments view and Exams' students+results view, each cropped to what that audience needs. The conceptual level answers 'what exists, and how does it relate?' — one single logical schema (tables, columns, relationships, rules) underneath all those different views. The internal level answers 'how is it physically stored?' — the actual files, indexes, and storage engine details the DBMS and DBA manage. In the weekend upgrade, ICT changed things ONLY at the internal level: which server the data lives on, how three big tables are physically stored, and which indexes exist. None of that touched the conceptual schema (the tables, columns, and relationships stayed logically identical) or the external views built on top of it, which is precisely why every application — the portal, Bursary's reports, Exams' summaries — kept working without a single line of code changing. This is physical data independence in action: a change confined entirely to the internal level, invisible to everything above it.
keyPoints: External — what a specific user group sees (many views)
Conceptual — what exists and how it relates (one logical schema)
Internal — how it's physically stored (one physical layout)
The weekend upgrade changed only the internal level, so nothing above it broke

theory.question: Explain the difference between additive and destructive schema change, using specific examples, and describe why a 3-tier architecture's middle tier is described as holding 'the rules and the credentials.'
theory.modelAnswer: Additive change extends a schema without removing or altering anything existing applications already depend on — adding a new column like email, creating a brand-new table, or adding a new index are all additive, and every existing view or application keeps working exactly as before. Destructive change removes or fundamentally alters something already in use — dropping a column a view depends on, renaming a table an application points at, or splitting a table that other queries JOIN against — and each of these breaks whatever was built on top of the thing that changed. The professional discipline this teaches is to design conservatively: extend outward rather than rewriting what's load-bearing, since the three-schema architecture only protects against storage-layer changes, not against a designer destructively altering the conceptual schema itself. In a 3-tier architecture, the middle tier (the application server) is described as holding 'the rules and the credentials' because users interact only with the browser or mobile app, which talks only to the application server — the application server is the sole layer that actually connects to the database, meaning it's the only place that needs the database credentials, and it's also where business logic (the rules about what a user is allowed to do) actually lives, rather than being scattered across every client device.
keyPoints: Additive: ADD COLUMN, new table, new index — nothing existing breaks
Destructive: DROP a used column, rename a table apps point at, split a joined table
Design conservatively: extend rather than rewrite
3-tier middle tier: sole database connection point, holds both business rules and credentials

chapters.title: Conceptual Data Modelling: The ER Model — Topic 2

cards.heading: The hostel system nobody modelled
cards.body:
A developer skips design entirely and goes straight to CREATE TABLE: one table, hostel_name and room_number stored right on each student's row.

Two weeks later: Room B12 somehow holds nine students. One student is registered in two hostels at once. Renaming a hall means editing 400 rows by hand. By mid-semester, it needs a full month-long rebuild.

Ten minutes on a whiteboard — before a single table existed — would have exposed every one of those defects. Drawing that whiteboard precisely, the right way, is this chapter's craft.

Every Nigerian undergraduate who's opened their hostel room to find an extra mattress on the floor and a total stranger's box under their bed already understands this failure in their bones.

cards.heading: Why model first: the design process
cards.body:
Building a database properly follows a pipeline, not a jump straight to SQL:

Mini-world (the office, the business, the need) → Requirements (interviews, forms, rules written down) → Conceptual design (an ER diagram — THIS chapter) → Logical design (relational schema — mapping it, Chapter 7) → Physical design (indexes, storage engines — Chapters 5 and 11).

Change is cheap on a diagram and expensive in a live database — erasing a wrong box costs nothing, but an ALTER TABLE on a live system with data in it is a real headache. And the Dean can't read SQL, but she can absolutely read a diagram and tell you if it's wrong.

cards.heading: The notation cheat sheet
cards.body:
ER diagrams (Chen notation) use a small, consistent shape language:

• Rectangle = **Entity** (STUDENT); double rectangle = **weak entity** (SCRIPT — depends on something else to exist)
• Diamond = **Relationship** (REGISTERS)
• Oval = **Attribute** (full_name); underlined oval = **key attribute** (matric_no); double oval = **multivalued** (phone — a student can have several); dashed oval = **derived** (age, computed from dob, usually not stored)
• Double line between an entity and a relationship = **total participation** — every instance MUST take part

**Cardinality** gets written on the connecting lines: 1:1 (DEPT–HEADS–LECTURER, one head per department), 1:N (PROGRAMME–ENROLS–STUDENT, one programme, many students), or M:N (STUDENT–REGISTERS–COURSE, many-to-many).

cards.heading: Entity or attribute? The working tests
cards.body:
Five quick questions settle almost every case:

• Does it have facts of its own we must store? → **Entity** (HOSTEL: warden, capacity)
• Do many things point at one of it? → Entity, stored once and referenced (400 students → one PROGRAMME)
• Is it a single fact about one thing? → **Attribute** (dob belongs to one STUDENT)
• Can one thing have several of it? → Multivalued attribute (a student's phone numbers)
• Is it computable from stored facts? → Derived — usually don't store it (age ← dob)

The hostel disaster in one line: HOSTEL was stored as an attribute (just a text field on the student) when it plainly has facts of its own — a warden, a capacity — and should have been its own entity.

cards.heading: Two questions that discipline every relationship
cards.body:
Every relationship needs two questions answered, precisely:

• **Cardinality** — how many, each way? 1:1 (a department has one head), 1:N (a programme has many students), M:N (students × courses).
• **Participation** — must everyone take part? Total (double line): every STUDENT must have a PROGRAMME. Partial: not every LECTURER teaches this session.

And relationships can own attributes: a course score doesn't belong to the student, and it doesn't belong to the course — it belongs to that specific student-course pairing, so it hangs off the REGISTERS relationship itself. Spotting these is the mark of a real designer. Answering cardinality/participation wrongly is exactly how Room B12 got nine occupants — nothing was enforcing a capacity limit anywhere.

Think of seating an Owambe: the couple's table is 1:1, the family table holding one whole gele squad is 1:N, and the small chops trays that circulate to EVERY table at once — that's M:N.

cards.heading: Building a model: the four moves
cards.body:
Any ER model gets built the same four-step way:

1. **Hunt the entities** — nouns with facts of their own; run the entity-or-attribute tests on each candidate.
2. Settle relationships and cardinalities — the M:N cases (like REGISTERS) are the ones that can't hide inside either entity.
3. **Attach attributes**, including the relationship's own — keys get underlined, phone is **multivalued**, store dob and derive age, score belongs to REGISTERS.
4. Walk every rule against the finished diagram — it's done when every rule is visibly enforced, or consciously deferred with a reason.

cards.heading: The complete Beacon model
cards.body:
Assembled from every rule above, Beacon University's full conceptual model:

DEPARTMENT (dept_id, dept_name) —1:N EMPLOYS→ LECTURER (staff_id, staff_name) —1:N TEACHES→ COURSE (course_id, course_code, title, units)
DEPARTMENT —1:N OFFERS→ PROGRAMME (programme_id, programme_name) —1:N ENROLS→ STUDENT (student_id, matric_no, full_name, dob, phone [**multivalued**])
STUDENT —M:N REGISTERS→ COURSE, with session, score and grade hanging off REGISTERS itself, not off either entity
STUDENT —1:N MAKES→ PAYMENT (payment_id, amount, paid_on)

Every box, diamond and oval on this diagram exists because one of the earlier tests demanded it.

visual.caption: The complete Beacon model — every box, diamond, and oval justified by one of the tests from this chapter.

cards.heading: The recursive relationship: when an entity relates to its own kind
cards.body:
Every relationship so far has connected two DIFFERENT entities — STUDENT to COURSE, DEPARTMENT to LECTURER. But sometimes an entity needs to relate to another instance of ITSELF, and that's a **recursive relationship** — genuinely one of the trickier ideas to spot in this whole chapter.

Beacon's course catalogue needs exactly this: CSC308 requires CSC201 as a prerequisite, which itself might require an even earlier course. That's COURSE connecting to COURSE, through a PREREQUISITE_OF relationship, and it's genuinely M:N — one course can have several prerequisites, and one course can BE a prerequisite for several other courses at once.

Other real examples: an EMPLOYEE who reports to another EMPLOYEE (their manager), a STUDENT who referred another STUDENT to Beacon, a PART made up of smaller PARTs. Same entity, drawn twice with a relationship diamond between the two copies, same M:N mapping rule from before applies: it becomes its own new table — course_prerequisites(course_id, prerequisite_id) — just with both foreign keys pointing back at the SAME table instead of two different ones.

cards.heading: Five rules: diagram to tables
cards.body:
Once the ER diagram is right, mapping it to real tables is mechanical — five rules, always in this order:

1. A strong entity becomes a table; its **key attribute** becomes the primary key.
2. A 1:N relationship becomes a foreign key on the N side (students carries programme_id).
3. A 1:1 relationship gets a foreign key on either side — prefer the total-participation side, and make it UNIQUE.
4. An M:N relationship becomes a brand-new table: foreign keys to both sides, plus the relationship's own attributes.
5. A **multivalued** attribute gets its own small table (student_phones(student_id, phone)).

Rule 4 does the heavy lifting — it's the one designers get wrong most often.

cards.heading: The M:N rule in action
cards.body:
STUDENT —M:N REGISTERS→ COURSE, carrying session and score. An M:N relationship simply cannot live inside either entity's table — cramming it into students or courses would mean repeating rows for every course a student takes, or vice versa.

So it becomes its own new table: registrations(student_id, course_id, session, score, grade) — one row per (student, course, session), carrying the relationship's own attributes, with student_id as a foreign key back to students and course_id as a foreign key back to courses.

This one move — turning an M:N relationship into its own table — is the heart of the entire mapping algorithm. Master this and the other four rules are easy by comparison.

steps.caption: Step 1 — The M:N relationship, with its own attributes.

shapes.label: This relationship can't live inside STUDENT's table or COURSE's table.

steps.caption: Step 2 — Rule 4: an M:N relationship becomes a brand-new table.

shapes.label: Foreign keys to both sides, plus the relationship's own attributes.

steps.caption: Step 3 — The result: one row per registration, keyed back to both parents.

quiz.question: In the hostel scenario, Room B12 ended up holding nine students with no way to catch it. What was the core modelling mistake?
options: HOSTEL was stored as an attribute instead of being modelled as its own entity
The database used the wrong storage engine
The developer forgot to add an index
STUDENT should have been a weak entity
quiz.explanation: HOSTEL clearly has facts of its own (a warden, a capacity) — it should have been modelled as its own entity, not just a text field bolted onto each student row. Without that, nothing could ever enforce a room's capacity.

quiz.question: A student can have several phone numbers on file. How is this represented in an ER diagram?
quiz.explanation: Multivalued attribute (drawn as a double oval) — the entity-or-attribute test for "can one thing have several?" points straight to this, same as a student's phone numbers.

quiz.question: A double line connecting STUDENT to the ENROLS relationship means what?
options: Total participation — every student must take part in this relationship
The attribute is derived, not stored
quiz.explanation: Total participation — a double line means every instance of that entity (every STUDENT) must take part; a single line (partial participation) means it's optional, like not every lecturer teaching this particular session.

quiz.question: A student's score in a specific course doesn't belong to STUDENT or to COURSE alone. Where does it belong?
options: It belongs to the REGISTERS relationship itself
It should be split evenly between both entities
quiz.explanation: The REGISTERS relationship itself — score describes the specific student-course pairing, not either entity alone, which is exactly the kind of relationship-owned attribute a good designer learns to spot.

quiz.question: Under the five mapping rules, how does an M:N relationship (like STUDENT–REGISTERS–COURSE) become tables?
options: It's added as extra columns on the STUDENT table
It's added as extra columns on the COURSE table
It becomes a brand-new table with foreign keys to both sides plus its own attributes
It's ignored — M:N relationships can't be mapped to relational tables
quiz.explanation: A new table — an M:N relationship can't live inside either entity's table without repeating rows, so it becomes its own table (like registrations) carrying foreign keys to both parents plus any attributes the relationship itself owns.

quiz.question: In a 1:N relationship where a PROGRAMME has many STUDENTs, which table gets the foreign key?
options: Neither — a new table is needed
Both tables get a foreign key
quiz.explanation: The N side — students carries programme_id as a foreign key. This is rule 2 of the five mapping rules: a 1:N relationship becomes a foreign key on the many side.

quiz.question: CSC308 requires CSC201 as a prerequisite, and CSC201 itself requires an even earlier course. How is this 'prerequisite' relationship best modelled?
options: A relationship between COURSE and a brand-new PREREQUISITE entity
A recursive M:N relationship, where COURSE relates to another instance of COURSE
It can't be modelled in a relational database at all
A 1:1 relationship between two separate course tables
quiz.explanation: This is a recursive relationship — COURSE relates to itself, since one course can have several prerequisites and one course can be a prerequisite for several others. It maps the same way any M:N relationship does, just with both foreign keys pointing back at the same table.

theory.question: Describe the four moves used to build any ER model, and use Beacon's STUDENT–REGISTERS–COURSE relationship to illustrate the second and third moves.
theory.modelAnswer: The four moves are: (1) hunt the entities — find nouns with facts of their own, using the entity-or-attribute tests; (2) settle relationships and cardinalities — decide how entities connect and in what numbers; (3) attach attributes, including any the relationship itself owns; (4) walk every rule against the finished diagram to confirm nothing was missed. For move two, STUDENT and COURSE connect through REGISTERS with an M:N cardinality — many students register for many courses, so this relationship can't be hidden inside either entity. For move three, attributes like session, score and grade don't describe a student alone or a course alone, they describe one specific student-course pairing — so they get attached directly to the REGISTERS relationship rather than to STUDENT or COURSE.
keyPoints: Hunt the entities (apply the tests)
Settle relationships & cardinalities (M:N for REGISTERS)
Attach attributes, including the relationship's own (session/score/grade on REGISTERS)
Walk every rule against the diagram

theory.question: State the five rules for mapping an ER diagram to relational tables, and explain in detail how the M:N rule applies to Beacon's STUDENT–REGISTERS–COURSE relationship.
theory.modelAnswer: The five rules are: (1) a strong entity becomes a table, with its key attribute as the primary key; (2) a 1:N relationship becomes a foreign key on the N side; (3) a 1:1 relationship gets a foreign key on either side, preferring the total-participation side, made UNIQUE; (4) an M:N relationship becomes a brand-new table with foreign keys to both sides plus the relationship's own attributes; (5) a multivalued attribute gets its own small table. Applying rule 4 to REGISTERS: since STUDENT and COURSE have an M:N relationship, it cannot be represented as extra columns on either table without repeating data. Instead it becomes a new registrations table with student_id and course_id as foreign keys pointing back to students and courses respectively, plus columns for session, score and grade — the attributes that belong to the relationship itself. This turns one many-to-many relationship into one clean new table, one row per actual registration.
keyPoints: Strong entity → table, key → primary key
1:N → FK on the N side
1:1 → FK on either side, prefer total side, UNIQUE
M:N → new table, FKs to both sides + relationship attributes
Multivalued → its own small table

cards.heading: The ghost registrations
cards.body:
Results week at Beacon. A routine count turns up something nobody wants to find: 61 registrations pointing at students who don't exist. Some are just mistyped student numbers — a finger slipped, a digit flipped. Others are applicants who got deleted after clearance, leaving their registrations orphaned behind them like a coat left on a chair after everyone went home.

61 grades. Completely unawardable — there's nobody real to award them to.

The table has columns. The table has rows. What it doesn't have is rules — its "foreign keys" were just ordinary numbers that nothing on earth was ever checking. Today's whole chapter is the iron rulebook that makes this exact disaster structurally impossible, with MySQL itself standing guard and enforcing every single one.

cards.heading: The anatomy of a relation
cards.body:
A relation (the formal name for a table) has four properties worth knowing precisely, because exam questions love asking for them by name. Every cell holds exactly one atomic value — no cramming three phone numbers into one box. Column order doesn't matter — programme_id before or after full_name changes nothing about what the table means. Row order doesn't matter either — a table isn't a queue, there's no "first" student. And every row must be unique — if two rows are 100% identical in every column, one of them is pointless.

The vocabulary: an attribute is a column (student_id, matric_no). A **tuple** is a row — one actual student, Amina Yusuf, sitting in the students table. **Degree** is how many attributes a relation has (4 columns = degree 4). **Cardinality** is how many tuples it currently holds (3 students = cardinality 3, and it changes every time someone registers or withdraws). And **domain** is the set of legal values for a column — matric_no's domain is "valid matric strings only," which is exactly why a phone number could never legally sit in that column.

cards.heading: Keys: every row's actual name
cards.body:
A **superkey** is ANY set of columns that's guaranteed unique — {student_id, full_name} counts, so does {matric_no, dob}, and honestly most superkeys are bloated and nobody actually wants to use them as-is.

A **candidate key** is a MINIMAL superkey — strip away any single column and it stops being unique. {student_id} alone is a candidate key. {matric_no} alone is too. But {student_id, full_name} is NOT a candidate key, because student_id alone was already doing the job — the full_name was just dead weight riding along for nothing.

One candidate key gets promoted to **primary key** (the row's official, chosen name). Every other candidate key that didn't get picked becomes an **alternate key**, enforced with **UNIQUE** instead of PRIMARY KEY. Beacon's students table has two real candidates — student_id and matric_no — and only one of them gets to wear the crown.

cards.heading: Choosing the primary key: stable, compact, meaningless
cards.body:
Not every **candidate key** deserves to be **primary key**, and getting this choice wrong haunts a design for years. A good primary key is **Stable** — it's never edited. Matric numbers occasionally need correcting (a typo at admission, a records-office fix); an auto-incrementing number never does, because nobody has an opinion about what a database's internal counter should say.

**Compact** — a primary key gets physically copied into every table that references it, and into every index built on it. A short integer copies cheap. A long composite string copies expensive, over and over, everywhere it's referenced.

**Meaningless** — values that encode real-world meaning invite real-world change, and change is exactly what a primary key can't tolerate.

The professional pattern, used everywhere in serious schema design: a **surrogate primary key** (student_id AUTO_INCREMENT — meaningless, stable, compact) PLUS the natural key kept as **UNIQUE** (matric_no — meaningful, human-readable, still enforced as unique, just not doing the heavy lifting as PK). And where identity genuinely IS a combination of things — a specific student in a specific course in a specific session — the key itself gets composite: registrations(student_id, course_id, session).

cards.heading: The two integrity rules
cards.body:
**Entity integrity**: the **primary key** is NEVER NULL and NEVER duplicated. Every single row must be addressable by its own unique, present key — a row with a NULL primary key is a row that can never be found again, and a duplicate primary key means two rows are both claiming to be the same specific thing.

**Referential integrity**: every foreign key points at a row that actually exists. This is the exact rule Beacon's 61 ghost registrations violated — student_id 9999 in the registrations table pointed at a student row that had already been deleted, and nothing was checking.
