(The same Friday has two more disasters waiting at 5 p.m. and 9 p.m. — those belong to the next topic, Transactions, Concurrency and Recovery. This topic is entirely about the first two: who's allowed in, and what happens when input becomes code.)

Both failures share the same root shape: a boundary that should have stopped something, and didn't. Today's job is building boundaries that actually hold.

cards.heading: Security: defence in depth
cards.body:
No single wall is trusted — the data sits behind concentric rings, and an attacker must defeat every one:

• **Authentication** — WHO are you? Strong passwords, least-privilege accounts.
• **Authorisation (DCL)** — WHAT may you do? GRANT / REVOKE, roles, views used as windows onto only what a role needs.
• **Input validation** — is this input SAFE? Parameterised queries stop SQL injection.
• **Encryption** — unreadable if stolen? **TLS** in transit, encryption at rest.

Beacon's noon disaster was a failure of the second ring: a leaver's account should have been REVOKEd the moment they left, not discovered weeks later still holding full admin rights.

cards.heading: Least privilege in practice: roles, GRANT/REVOKE, and the leaver drill
cards.body:
The **principle of least privilege**: every account gets EXACTLY what its job needs, and nothing more — not "probably won't need it," not "just in case," exactly what's required and no further.

In practice, this means designing real role accounts for real jobs: a Bursary clerk's account can SELECT and UPDATE payments, but has no business anywhere near results. An Exams officer's account can touch results, but not payments. Neither account can run DDL — no ordinary clerk should be able to DROP a table. `GRANT SELECT, UPDATE ON payments TO 'bursary_clerk'@'%';` grants exactly one privilege on exactly one table to exactly one role.

The leaver drill, live: `REVOKE ALL PRIVILEGES ON *.* FROM 'departed_staff'@'%';` — then, on that SAME still-open connection the departed staff member was already using, attempt one more query. It's denied, immediately, mid-session. This is exactly what should have happened to Beacon's noon leaver, on the day they actually left, not weeks later after damage was already done.

cards.heading: SQL injection — the one rule that stops it
cards.body:
The world's most famous database vulnerability has a single cause. Vulnerable code glues user input straight into SQL text: `query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '" + input + "';"`. Type `' OR '1'='1` into the name box, and the database actually receives `SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '' OR '1'='1';` — always true, every row returned. The attacker's text became CODE, not data.

The fix: a **parameterised query** (prepared statement) — `query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = ?"; execute(query, [input])`. The same malicious input arrives as one harmless string value, never parsed as SQL. Code and data stay in separate lanes. The one rule: never build SQL by string concatenation — always parameterise.

It's the database equivalent of a classic scam-format trick — a few extra characters slipped into an ordinary-looking sentence quietly change what it actually means, except here the "sentence" is your SQL query and the "scam" hands over the whole users table.

The database version of the classic scam-format trick already flagged back in Module 1's cybersecurity material — a few extra characters slipped into an ordinary-looking input quietly change what the whole sentence actually means.

cards.heading: Views as the scalpel of authorisation, plus TLS and encryption at rest
cards.body:
GRANT and REVOKE work at the table level — all of a table's columns, or none. But real jobs rarely need ALL of a table. A views-based grant is the scalpel: `CREATE VIEW bursary_view AS SELECT student_id, full_name, amount_paid FROM students JOIN payments ...;` then `GRANT SELECT ON bursary_view TO 'bursary_clerk'@'%';` — the clerk can query the view freely, but has no access to the underlying students or payments tables directly, and never sees a single column the view didn't deliberately expose.

Two more layers, quickly: **TLS** encrypts data IN TRANSIT — while it's travelling across the network between a client and the server, so nobody sniffing the connection can read it. **Encryption** at rest protects data SITTING on disk — if someone steals the physical hard drive or an unauthorised backup copy, the files are unreadable without the key.

Neither one protects against everything: TLS does nothing once data has already arrived and been decrypted at its destination; encryption at rest does nothing against an attacker who's already authenticated as a legitimate, over-privileged user. Layers, again — never just one.

quiz.question: In the defence-in-depth model, which layer specifically answers the question "WHAT may you do?"
quiz.explanation: Authorisation (DCL) — implemented with GRANT/REVOKE, roles, and views. Authentication answers "who are you?", validation asks "is this input safe?", and encryption asks "is it unreadable if stolen?"

quiz.question: What is the single rule that prevents SQL injection?
options: Always use a stronger admin password
Never build SQL by string concatenation — always parameterise
quiz.explanation: Never build SQL by gluing in user input as text — always use a parameterised query, so input is bound as DATA and can never be parsed as CODE, no matter what the attacker types.

quiz.question: A Bursary clerk's account is granted SELECT and UPDATE on the payments table only, with no access to results and no ability to run DDL. What principle does this design follow?
quiz.explanation: Least privilege — the account gets exactly what its job requires (payments access) and nothing more, not broad access 'just in case.'

quiz.question: In the leaver drill, REVOKE ALL is run on a departed staff account. What happens to a query attempted on that account's ALREADY-OPEN connection immediately afterward?
options: It succeeds, since the connection was already established
It's denied immediately — the revoke takes effect on the next query, even on an existing open session
Nothing happens until the connection is manually closed and reopened
quiz.explanation: REVOKE takes effect immediately — the next query attempted on that connection is denied, exactly the drill that should have happened to Beacon's noon leaver the day they actually left.

quiz.question: Why is a views-based grant described as 'the scalpel' of authorisation, compared to a plain table-level GRANT?
options: Views are always faster than direct table access
A view can expose exactly the columns and rows a role needs, while a table-level GRANT is all-or-nothing across every column
Views don't require any GRANT at all
Views are only used for reporting, never for security
quiz.explanation: A table-level GRANT gives access to all of a table's columns or none; a view can be built to expose only specific columns and rows, giving precise, surgical control over exactly what a role can see.

quiz.question: What does encryption at rest specifically protect against, that TLS in transit does not?
options: Nothing — they protect against the exact same threat
Someone stealing the physical disk or an unauthorised backup copy, where the data is unreadable without the key even though it's not moving across a network
quiz.explanation: Encryption at rest protects data sitting on disk (e.g. a stolen drive or backup), which TLS — protecting only data in transit across a network — has no bearing on at all.

theory.question: Explain the principle of least privilege and design a simple role scheme for Beacon's Bursary and Exams offices, naming what each role can and cannot do.
theory.modelAnswer: The principle of least privilege states that every account should be granted exactly the access its job requires, and nothing more — not broad access granted 'just in case' it might be needed later. Applied to Beacon: a Bursary clerk role would be granted SELECT and UPDATE on the payments table only, since their job is processing and checking payment records — they would have no access whatsoever to the results table, since exam scores are outside their responsibility, and no ability to run DDL statements like CREATE or DROP, since altering the database's structure is a DBA function, not a clerical one. An Exams officer role would be the mirror image: SELECT and UPDATE on results, no access to payments, no DDL rights. Neither role would be granted DELETE on their respective tables unless record removal was a genuine, regular part of that job, and neither would have any GRANT or REVOKE rights themselves, since managing other accounts' privileges is a DBA-level responsibility, not something either operational role needs to do their actual job.
keyPoints: Least privilege: exactly what the job needs, nothing more
Bursary role: SELECT/UPDATE on payments only, no results access, no DDL
Exams role: SELECT/UPDATE on results only, no payments access, no DDL
Neither role gets GRANT/REVOKE rights — that's a DBA responsibility

theory.question: Explain SQL injection precisely — why does the input become executable code? — and explain why filtering out bad characters fails while parameterisation succeeds.
theory.modelAnswer: SQL injection happens when user input is glued directly into SQL text through string concatenation, rather than being kept separate from the query's actual structure. When a login check builds a query like `"SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '" + input + "';"`, and an attacker types `' OR '1'='1` as the input, the database doesn't receive a name to search for — it receives an entirely restructured SQL statement, because the attacker's quote character closed the intended string early, and the rest of their input became a new, always-true condition that gets parsed as actual SQL syntax. The input became executable code because the database engine has no way to distinguish 'text the programmer wrote' from 'text the attacker supplied' once they've been concatenated into one string — both look identical to the SQL parser. Filtering out bad characters fails because it's a blacklist approach trying to anticipate every possible dangerous pattern in advance, and attackers routinely find characters, encodings, or patterns the filter didn't think to block. Parameterisation succeeds because it's a fundamentally different mechanism, not a better filter: the query structure and the user's input are sent to the database separately, with the input always bound as a literal DATA value that can never be reinterpreted as SQL syntax, no matter what characters it contains — the ' OR '1'='1 trick becomes a harmless, literal search string instead of a structural change to the query.
keyPoints: Injection: user input concatenated directly into SQL text, becoming part of the query's structure
Attacker's quote character closes the intended string early, turning input into new SQL syntax
Filtering bad characters = an incomplete blacklist, always guessable around
Parameterisation: input bound as data, never parsed as code — a mechanism change, not a better filter

cards.heading: One weekend, two more disasters
cards.body:
The same bad Friday, later on. 5 p.m.: two clerks confirm the same award at once — one silently overwrites the other. This is Chapter 4's very first scenario at Beacon, unfixed for seven chapters. Today it finally dies. 9 p.m.: a power cut kills the server mid-transaction.

(Noon's leaver and 3 p.m.'s injection attack already got dealt with in the previous topic, Securing the Database. This topic picks up from here: what happens when two things happen at once, and what happens when everything stops happening at all.)

Both of these are the database defending itself against a different enemy than security does — not a malicious outsider, but ordinary contention and ordinary catastrophe, which arrive eventually no matter how well-behaved every single user is.

cards.heading: Transactions and ACID
cards.body:
A transaction is all-or-nothing work, wrapped in `START TRANSACTION; ... COMMIT;` (or `ROLLBACK` to abandon it entirely) — the second seatbelt, after Chapter 9's SELECT-first pattern for safe writes. Four guarantees make it trustworthy:

• **Atomicity** — all steps happen, or none do (a transfer never debits without crediting)
• **Consistency** — the database moves between valid states (constraints hold before and after)
• **Isolation** — concurrent transactions don't corrupt each other (as if they ran one at a time)
• **Durability** — committed means it survives a crash (the write is on disk, permanently)

COMMIT means durable and permanent. ROLLBACK means it never happened at all.

cards.heading: The lost update: Chapter 4's ghost, named
cards.body:
Two clerks both update a hall's seat count at once. Clerk A adds 40 units, Clerk B adds 3. Both READ seats → 100 before either writes.

Clerk A computes 100+40=140, writes seats=140. Clerk B — still working from the 100 it read earlier, before A's write — computes 100+3=103, writes seats=103, overwriting A's change completely.

Clerk A's +40 vanished. The final answer should be 143; it's 103. This is the exact unnamed bug from Chapter 4's opening night at Beacon, finally given its technical name: the **lost update**. It happens whenever two transactions' reads and writes interleave destructively.

cards.heading: The cure: locking and isolation levels
cards.body:
**Two-phase locking (2PL)** serialises the clash: Clerk A locks seats, reads 100, writes 140, commits, releasing the lock. Clerk B was forced to WAIT for that lock — so B only reads 140 (the up-to-date value) after A finishes, computes 140+3=143, and writes seats=143. Correct, this time.

**Isolation** levels let you dial how much clashing to prevent, against how much speed: READ UNCOMMITTED (fastest, least safe) → READ COMMITTED → REPEATABLE READ (MySQL/InnoDB's default) → SERIALIZABLE (safest, slowest). Higher isolation means fewer anomalies but more locking and less concurrency — pick the LOWEST level that's still correct for your workload.

cards.heading: Recovery: surviving the crash
cards.body:
**Durability**'s actual machinery: the **write-ahead log** records every change FIRST, before it's applied to the real data — so a crash is always recoverable.

Picture a timeline: a **checkpoint** (the last known-good snapshot on disk), then T1 commits, T2 commits, T3 is still running... then CRASH. Recovery does two things: **REDO** the committed work (replay T1 and T2 from the log, so nothing committed is ever lost) and **UNDO** the unfinished work (roll back T3, so nothing half-done survives).

This is exactly what would have saved Beacon's 9 p.m. power cut — the transaction in flight gets cleanly undone, not left in a broken half-state.

This is the actual logic behind every Nigerian household's inverter setup: the point was never to stop NEPA from ever failing — it's to make sure nothing important gets lost the exact second the light goes.

cards.heading: Why logs and backups defend against different disasters
cards.body:
The course's closing question: why do the log and the backup defend against different disasters, if they're both about "not losing data"?

The **write-ahead log** defends against a crash on the SAME disk — the data is still physically there, just interrupted mid-write, and replaying the log (**REDO**/**UNDO**) puts it back in a correct state.

A backup defends against something the log can't fix at all — the disk itself being destroyed, corrupted, or stolen. If there's no separate copy elsewhere, no amount of log replay can recover data that no longer physically exists. Real durability needs both: a log for interrupted work, a backup for catastrophic loss.

cards.heading: The whole course, in one database
cards.body:
Everything built across this course converges on one professional artefact:

Chapters 1-3: foundations — information, capture, indexing, privacy.
Chapters 4-5: database systems and architecture.
Chapters 6-8: design — the ER model, relational rules, semi-structured data.
Chapters 9-11: working with data — SQL, normalisation, optimisation.
Chapter 12: defending it — security, transactions, recovery.

Beacon University began this course drowning in spreadsheets, losing 43 registrations to a silent overwrite. By the end, you're the one who can build the system that saves it — conceived, built, queried, tuned, and defended, one database at a time.

quiz.question: The 5 p.m. clash in this chapter's opening scenario (two clerks overwriting each other's update) is the same bug first seen at the very start of the course. What is it called?
quiz.explanation: The lost update — first seen unnamed as Chapter 4's opening scenario, now formally named and finally cured with locking, eleven chapters later.

quiz.question: Which ACID property specifically guarantees that once a transaction commits, it survives a crash?
quiz.explanation: Durability — committed means the write is on disk, permanently. Atomicity is all-or-nothing steps, Consistency keeps the database in valid states, and Isolation stops concurrent transactions from corrupting each other.

quiz.question: In the two-phase locking cure, why does Clerk B end up writing the CORRECT seats=143 instead of repeating the lost update?
options: B skips reading the value entirely
B has to wait for A's lock to release, so B reads the up-to-date value (140), not the stale one
The database automatically adds both clerks' numbers together
quiz.explanation: B is forced to wait for A's lock to release before it can even read seats — so by the time B reads, it sees A's committed value (140), computes 140+3=143 correctly, instead of working from a stale value like before.

quiz.question: Why does a database need BOTH a write-ahead log AND separate backups, if both exist to prevent data loss?
options: They're redundant — either one alone is sufficient
The log recovers interrupted work on the same disk after a crash; a backup protects against the disk itself being lost or destroyed, which no log can fix
Backups are only needed for very old database systems
The log is for security, backups are for performance
quiz.explanation: They defend against different disaster classes — the log lets you REDO/UNDO work after a crash because the data is still physically on the same disk, while a backup is the only defence if that disk itself is destroyed or corrupted entirely.

quiz.question: MySQL/InnoDB defaults to which isolation level?
quiz.explanation: REPEATABLE READ is InnoDB's default — higher isolation than READ COMMITTED, but not as strict (or as slow) as SERIALIZABLE, a deliberate middle-ground default for typical workloads.

quiz.question: After a crash, recovery finds T1 and T2 already committed, and T3 still running when the crash hit. What does recovery do to each?
options: REDO both T1 and T2; REDO T3 as well
REDO T1 and T2 (replay their committed work); UNDO T3 (roll back the unfinished transaction)
REDO T3 only; ignore T1 and T2
quiz.explanation: REDO applies to committed work (T1, T2) so nothing committed is ever lost; UNDO applies to unfinished work (T3) so nothing half-done survives the crash.

theory.question: Using the Clerk A / Clerk B seat-count example, explain exactly what a lost update is and why 'read first, write second' causes it — then explain how two-phase locking prevents it from happening again.
theory.modelAnswer: A lost update happens when two transactions both read the same value before either one writes, then both compute a new value based on that same stale read. In the example, both Clerk A and Clerk B read seats=100. Clerk A computes 140 and writes it. Clerk B, still working from the 100 it read earlier (not A's new 140), computes 103 and writes that — silently overwriting A's change. The final value should be 143 (100+40+3) but ends up being 103, because A's +40 update was completely lost. Two-phase locking prevents this by making Clerk B wait until Clerk A's transaction fully commits and releases its lock before Clerk B is even allowed to read the value. This means B reads the up-to-date value of 140, not the stale 100, so its calculation correctly produces 143 instead of repeating the same mistake.
keyPoints: Both transactions read the same stale value before either writes
The second write silently overwrites the first transaction's change
Lost update: final value is wrong because one update never took effect
Two-phase locking forces the second transaction to wait, so it reads the updated value

theory.question: Explain the four ACID guarantees, and describe specifically how the write-ahead log's REDO mechanism is what actually delivers on the Durability guarantee.
theory.modelAnswer: ACID's four guarantees are: Atomicity (all the steps in a transaction happen, or none do — a transfer never debits one account without crediting the other), Consistency (the database only ever moves between valid states, with all constraints holding before and after), Isolation (concurrent transactions don't corrupt each other, behaving as if they ran one at a time), and Durability (once a transaction commits, it survives a crash). Durability is delivered in practice by the write-ahead log: every change is written to the log FIRST, before it's applied to the actual data. If the server crashes after a transaction has committed but before all its changes were fully written to the main data files, recovery replays (REDOes) that committed work from the log, so nothing that was committed is ever actually lost — the log is the mechanism that makes the Durability promise literally true.
keyPoints: Atomicity — all steps or none
Consistency — valid states before and after
Isolation — concurrent transactions don't corrupt each other
Durability — committed survives a crash
Write-ahead log records changes first; REDO replays committed work after a crash, delivering Durability
